dataset.description: The research grant creates new knowledge in the assessment of the technical condition of marine structures' concrete using non-destructive testing (NDT) methods, including conducting in-depth research with the novel drilling resistance method, which is rarely used in practice so far. Concrete in marine structures is subjected to aggressive environmental conditions, including exposure to chlorides, sulfates, and freezing, resulting in damage to the concrete. Up to date there is no methodology for damage assessment using NDT methods has been developed so far. Within the grant, concrete intended for marine structures will be manufactured, aged in aggressive environment, and NDT methods for assessing concrete durability will be applied and validated. The concrete will be examined using ultrasonic pulse velocity tester, rebound hammer, and the Windsor probe test, and an innovative method will be developed and validated to assess the condition of concrete layer-by-layer – resistance to drilling. Based on the results obtained, a methodology will be developed for assessing the durability of marine structures\' concrete, allowing for rapid assessment of the material\'s technical condition and degree of damage. The grant will establish a research group that brings together scientists from RTU and its cooperation partner RTU Latvian Maritime Academy. The grant also includes international collaboration with Brunel University London (UK) and involves students in the research.

dmp.description:
The research project “Methodology for Non-Destructive Testing of Marine Concrete Durability” was designed to address a clearly identified scientific and practical gap: the absence of a validated, layer-by-layer non-destructive testing (NDT) methodology specifically tailored to marine concrete exposed to aggressive environmental conditions.
Concrete in marine and hydrotechnical structures is subjected to chloride ingress (XS exposure classes), freeze–thaw action (XF classes), cyclic wetting–drying, and sulfate exposure. These mechanisms lead to depth-dependent deterioration, reinforcement cover degradation, and progressive durability loss. Existing standardised NDT methods (e.g., ultrasonic pulse velocity, rebound hammer, penetration resistance) provide primarily surface-weighted or averaged material responses and do not enable reliable profiling of concrete condition with depth. As confirmed by the final scientific report, no comprehensive methodology for durability-oriented assessment of marine concrete using combined NDT approaches had been previously developed.
The Project successfully developed and validated an integrated methodology combining conventional NDT techniques with an advanced drilling resistance (DR) approach. The DR method was adapted for concrete and systematically investigated as a minimally invasive, semi-destructive technique capable of:
  • identifying weakened surface layers,
  • evaluating strength gradients within the reinforcement cover zone,
  • quantifying the influence of moisture state on mechanical response,
  • improving in-situ strength prediction models using force- and energy-based parameters.
The research programme included:
  • production of marine concrete mixtures (C30–C50) corresponding to EN 206 exposure classes XS and XF,
  • laboratory ageing under aggressive simulated marine conditions,
  • systematic testing under both dry and saturated states,
  • statistical correlation of NDT indicators with compressive strength,
  • development of energy-based interpretation models for drilling resistance data,
  • validation through in-situ investigations on real marine structures.
More than 300 drilling tests were performed across multiple concrete types and moisture conditions, generating a comprehensive experimental dataset. The final outcome of the Project is a scientifically validated methodology for durability-oriented NDT assessment of marine concrete structures.
The purpose of this Data Management Plan (DMP) is to ensure that all research data generated during the Project — including laboratory measurements, drilling resistance datasets (force, torque, power, rotational speed), ultrasonic pulse velocity results, rebound hardness data, compressive strength tests, statistical analyses, field test results, and associated documentation — are:
  • properly structured and documented,
  • stored securely and preserved long-term,
  • accessible in accordance with FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable),
  • compliant with institutional and funding body requirements,
  • reusable for future research, international collaboration, standardisation activities, and development of next-generation NDT methodologies.
The DMP also ensures traceability between raw data, processed datasets, published results, and the developed NDT methodology. Given the scientific novelty of the drilling resistance application and the potential for future standardisation, the generated datasets represent a valuable resource for continued research development at national and international levels.
The Project established an interdisciplinary research group involving Riga Technical University and RTU Latvian Maritime Academy, with international collaboration partners and active student involvement. The data generated form the foundation for ongoing doctoral research, submitted international project proposals, and further development of semi-destructive NDT techniques for marine infrastructure durability assessment.
